Jump to proposal from 2025-04-25 https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-2828236219

---

Yes, I know I go against all WordPress, Drupal etc - but... development functionality is helpful for developers in development environment, where you install it, test it, configure it, write installation scripts etc.

Every kind of new modules, new themes, new x - you need it only in development and those must not be available in production (and in any other) environment. For any sensible application, it most be not allowed to develop in production.

I need to admit, that as a pen-tester I like those for sure :)

comments.body: When looking at this from both a security and software engineering lens, I agree that developer functionality shouldn't be available in production instances of an application. It seems obvious that exposing unnecessary developer functions in production for the sake of convenience exposes the application to unnecessary security risk but I couldn't find a CWE expression of this.

There are these related requirements:

> 14.1.6 | Verify that all unneeded features, documentation, sample applications and configurations are removed.
> 14.1.7 | Verify that production environment does not include test code.
I would like to send clear message as separate requirement, but it can be merged to 14.1.6.
@elarlang what would your suggested wording be?

> @elarlang what would your suggested wording be?

that is nice and complicated question :) Where goes the line - if installing new module is not ok, but configuring new webform with all the fields and logic is ok.

Maybe we could build the requirement around the idea of "program code integrity" - whatever was sent to production environment and is expected to be updated only via update process should not be changed by the application functionality (e.g. installing new modules, new themes, new whatever-program-code)

So I am not exactly sure what you are referring to on top of 14.1.6 and 14.1.7...

Can you be any more specific? "program code integrity" sounds a bit like 14.1.5 and also a a little like 14.1.1 and 14.1.3.

It does kinda feel like we have this covered @elarlang unless there is a missing perspective here?

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.1.1** | Verify that the application build and deployment processes are performed in a secure and repeatable way, such as CI / CD automation, automated configuration management, and automated deployment scripts. | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| **14.1.3** | [MODIFIED] Verify that configuration hardening is performed on all 3rd party products, libraries, frameworks and services as per their individual recommendations. | | ✓ | ✓ | 16 |
| **14.1.5** | [MODIFIED] Verify that deployed environments are short lived and frequently redeployed to a "known good" but updated state. Alternatively, long lived environments should use some form of "drift prevention" to ensure that deployed configurations are not changed to an insecure state. | | | ✓ | |

Those 14.1 requirements are more for deployment (and may be removed as out-of-scope for that). I try to get solution - when deployment to production is done, that application does not contain functionality (like upload new module, write your own program code) which can change deployed program code.
ISO 27001:2022 Annex A Control 8.31 still mandates the "Separation of Development, Test and Production Environments".
Separate environments are different topic. Different environment does not remove development functionality from production.

> Those 14.1 requirements are more for deployment (and may be removed as out-of-scope for that). I try to get solution - when deployment to production is done, that application does not contain functionality (like upload new module, write your own program code) which can change deployed program code.

Ok if I understand you correctly you are saying that if an app is like a "[Content Management System](https://kinsta.com/knowledgebase/content-management-system/)" (CMS) then that is a risk.

I am not sure that we can outright ban that as some applications are deliberately built that way. Maybe we can ban it but for L3 only?

@elarlang

Yes, CMS usually has the risk.

But. That's the case - it's _content_ management system and should not change the functionality in production environment if the application is used as information system (provides authentication for other users) and code-base changes actually are developed, committed and then transferred to production (so there should be no need to make/allow changes on production environment code).

The line there is thin and that's why we have the issue here - to understand, does the requirement makes sense or there are too big side-effects. So far I'm convinced we need the requirement.
Are you differentiating between content and functionality? I still think it is a tricky one that breaks various use cases. Would you be satisfied with a L3 requirement?

Level 3 is not the case here, as classical CMS most likely is not used as Level 3 application.

Based on by pen-testing experience, it should be level 2, just need to find (sound easy) correct wording.

> Level 3 is not the case here, as classical CMS most likely is not used as Level 3 application.
> 
> Based on by pen-testing experience, it should be level 2, just need to find (sound easy) correct wording.

I don't know how to do this without prohibiting something like wordpress. Do you have any ideas?
Ping @elarlang :)

> I don't know how to do this without prohibiting something like wordpress. Do you have any ideas?

Point is covered in comment: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issue-1470146918

If WordPress, Drupal, whoever have used risky architecture, it does not mean we need to accept the risk for everyone and everything for the future. Our goal should be sending the message.

And after re-reading it all, just need to point out my main goal or idea behind the issue.

From https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1564378015

> whatever was sent to production environment and is expected to be updated only via update process should not be changed by the application functionality (e.g. installing new modules, new themes, new whatever-program-code)
Ok so you are saying that CMS functionality in production is prohibited for L2 and above?
Well, not really... CMS stands for Content Management System. If this application is able to change it's own code, is it a content?
Ok so static content would be acceptable but dynamic content such as code and scripts would not be ok?

I think the word "dynamic" in CMS context is a bit confusing, as all content (articles, uploaded images etc) can be called dynamic.

Reusing this phrase
> whatever was sent to production environment and is expected to be updated only via update process should not be changed by the application functionality (e.g. installing new modules, new themes, new whatever-program-code)

So are we thinking like this:

> Verify that it is not possible to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production but rather only via the standard update/build process

Yes. The question is - should we limit it only for the functionality and code, which moves to production via update and build process.


... and this "/"

What else would you add?

 (clearly I have an inclination/addition towards slashes... 🤦🤦🤦🤦)
Nothing else. With mentioned limitation we should keep everything in place and point out "too kind permissions" which are not needed for the application (but are well used by attackers).

So you still want to add the requirement?

> Verify that it is not possible to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production but rather only via the standard update or build process
Yes, that seems nice :) Let's leave it for review for some time.

Condlusion and proposal:

* Category: V14.1 Build and Deploy
* Level: 2
* CWE: - (any proposals? [CWE-732](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/732.html)?)

Category - it's kind of fits to new "V14.7 Web or Application Server Configuration" as well, but I think in this situation proper and strict configuration for program code should be result of deployment (not a result of correct server configuration).


Proposal at the moment:
| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.1.X** | [ADDED] Verify that it is not possible to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production but rather only via the standard update or build process. | | ✓ | ✓ | |


We also heave similar requirement which says that unneeded features should be removed. It makes sense to answer future questions here - why we need separate one. Current 14.1.6 is important/supporting part to the new requirement, and it requires to not provide functionality in UI for making changes in program code (like installing new modules, themes, whatever components). We need separate one as second layer of defense, that even if the UI is there, there are no permissions on the server side to overwrite existing or add new program code. Also, strict permission setup must avoid adding new or overwriting existing code in case of some vulnerability as 2nd layer of defense.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.1.6** | [MOVED FROM 14.2.2] Verify that all unneeded features, documentation, sample applications and configurations are removed. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 1002 |

I think 14.1.6 implies a kinda of hardening/minification of the application to only what is needed in production.

Thinking more about the new requirement, it almost feels more like a design requirement than anything else:

> [ADDED] Verify that the application does not include the ability to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production. Code or functionality changes should only take place via the standard update or build process.

What do you think @elarlang 

Do we need a secure design chapter?

Proposed new requirement for me it's clear post-deploy-configuration - protect your program code from overwriting by strict permissions.

14.1.6 is more - don't provide unneeded features, it's not about configuration.

For new proposed requirement I don't think it suits to "secure design" section. Do we need it general - I don't know. If we have clear criteria what kind of requirement belongs there and we have enough requirements to match those criteria, then we can create it.

So @elarlang I think the requirement being added here is not a post-deploy configuration. To me it is preventing this sort of functionality being designed and implemented into the application itself it is just something which can probably not be made secure for higher assurance levels.
I think we have some fundamental differences how to look at it, because I would like to repeat my previous comment here again: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1751670400

Perhaps but I still don't quite get what you are thinking here. You keep saying the following:

> Whatever was sent to production environment and is expected to be updated only via update process should not be changed by the application functionality (e.g. installing new modules, new themes, new whatever-program-code)

To me, application functionality is something that is designed in and therefore me have to require that functionality like that is not designed into the application.

You talk elsewhere about permissions but I think is theoretically also covered by the proposed requirement.

If we ignore secure design for now, do you think that the [proposed requirement from here](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1752631559) belongs in 14.1?

> [ADDED] Verify that the application does not include the ability to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production. Code or functionality changes should only take place via the standard update or build process.

> To me, application functionality is something that is designed in and therefore me have to require that functionality like that is not designed into the application.

I think I watch your "functionality is something that is designed in" as "unneeded feature" for production and that is why I said in https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1751670400 it is covered by 14.1.6 to just point out the difference between proposed new requirement and 14.1.6:

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.1.6** | [MOVED FROM 14.2.2] Verify that all unneeded features, documentation, sample applications and configurations are removed. | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | 1002 |


and if unneeded feature is covered by 14.1.6, then rest of it is for permissions - if there is no functionality for that (or this part is fixed), then if permissions allow, then there is still problem to solve.

| # | Description | L1 | L2 | L3 | CWE |
| :---: | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **14.1.X** | [ADDED] Verify that it is not possible to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production but rather only via the standard update or build process. | | ✓ | ✓ | |

Does this makes sense?

> If we ignore secure design for now, do you think that the proposed requirement from here belongs in 14.1?

Yes, I think it suits to 14.1
I'm ok with current wording, but now watching it.. is it ok do have negative requirement?
Good, let's go with that.
Ok so merge it please @elarlang :)

> Ok so merge it please @elarlang :)

but you just marked PR to be ready without commiting new version?
![Untitled](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/assets/13623828/64e7088b-70e2-4462-8e10-636803bbcbca)

That should have sorted it out now...
Sorry

As it stands now:

_13.4.3 Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update or build process and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism._

This is more of a process and cannot really be verified in a running application. This requires verifying developer processes or verifying a DevOps pipeline or similar. **_I suggest it go away._** 

And as a side note, I mostly agree with this requirement. I just don't think it's ASVS material. It's not always a real risk, it does not necessarily lead to insecure software like SQLi, even if it is a sloppy process.
This is for sure is not about the process. Please read the issue first.

> This is for sure is not about the process. Please read the issue first

Well, I did read the issue. "build process" is directly in the requirement. 

13.4.3 Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update or **_build process_** and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism.

Maybe the text needs to change, because as is - regardless of the previous discussion - it currently reads like a process requirement and is not really verifiable _as is_.

Also, there are many application services - like Salesforce and similar - where adding new functionality in production is part of the service they offer. I can literally paste new code into SalesForce and push it live directly through application functionality and I do not need to go through any kind of "build process".

I read a full requirement, and for me it is not a process requirement. It says, that application must not be able to modify it's own code and it is allowed only via standard update or build process.

If you want to remove those, you'll come probably in other thread and say that requirements are too abstract without describing too much.

> Also, there are many application services - like Salesforce and similar - where adding new functionality in production is part of the service they offer. I can literally paste new code into SalesForce and push it live directly through application functionality and I do not need to go through any kind of "build process".

In this situation I consider it as "standard update process" for this functionality. The requirement is "against" WordPress, Drupal etc functionality, that basically provide development tools into production.

So [2 days ago you explained](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2953#issuecomment-2810512159), that we need this requirement:
> 13.4.6 Verify that mechanisms are in place to detect and respond to configuration drift in deployed environments. This may include using immutable infrastructure, automated redeployment from a secure baseline, or drift detection tools that compare current state against approved configurations.

How does it match with proposing to remove the requirement that disallows an application from modifying its own code?

The current text reads like a process requirement.
* **_standard update or build process_** naturally evokes change‑management workflows, CI/CD, release approvals, etc.—all outside the running application.
* A pentester or assessor reading 13.4.3 today would have to interview DevOps staff or audit a pipeline to “verify” compliance. That takes us out of application verification and into SDLC/process territory, which ASVS usually keeps away from.

If you want to keep this in, I'd suggest a change to make it more verifiable that is admittedly a more negative requirement,

_13.4.3 Verify that the running application — including its runtime environment, administration interfaces, and APIs — cannot modify its own executable code or compiled artifacts unless the change is delivered through an authenticated, integrity‑protected update mechanism (e.g, signed packages, secured CI/CD deployment, or the platform’s native version‑controlled update channel)._

> So [2 days ago you explained](https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2953#issuecomment-2810512159), that we need this requirement:
> 
> > 13.4.6 Verify that mechanisms are in place to detect and respond to configuration drift in deployed environments. This may include using immutable infrastructure, automated redeployment from a secure baseline, or drift detection tools that compare current state against approved configurations.
> 
> How does it match with proposing to remove the requirement that disallows an application from modifying its own code?

I am mostly just trying to support other volunteers who are making suggestions. If we want to keep infrastructure out of scope, I can see this one going away as well. Or maybe keep it in for intrusion detection. But yea, both of these are _drifting_ away from core application security, no pun intended.

> And as a side note, I mostly agree with this requirement. I just don't think it's ASVS material. It's not always a real risk, it does not necessarily lead to insecure software like SQLi, even if it is a sloppy process.

about this one - if you can install own-controlled module to the application, it gives quite possibly the how to execute your own code.

I have tested and report it enough to say - this requirement stays and it is not a subject to be removed. If there is anything confusing in the wording, it can be always improved,

The requirement don't say a word what the build pipeline need to do, it only says, that this is one of the allowed method to get the application installed.

---

If you put new proposal in place, please provide all the changes you made. You force me _every time_ to make the diff, analyze what can be the reasons behind that and assume what is the idea there. It takes a lot of time and the time comes from "moving forward pool".

The current requirement was not about the process, but your new proposal sets conditions for build process.

---

For background:

https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1775127981 - original proposal, but negative requirement

> Verify that it is not possible to make changes to application code or functionality directly in production but rather only via the standard update or build process.

https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-1775524706 - requirement written to be positive requirement

> Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update or build process and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism.

> If you put new proposal in place, please provide all the changes you made. You force me every time to make the diff, analyze what can be the reasons behind that and assume what is the idea there. It takes a lot of time and the time comes from "moving forward pool".

This is my whole point. You should not have to do that. If the requirement is so confusing that you need to go back and do deep diff research, then developers reading the requirement will have to do the same - and therefor its not clear enough. _Good requirements should stand strong as they are._ And this one does not. It smells of process. Like really obviously it smells of process, it's in the requirement text itself. 

So I totally support you wanting to keep it in, I just think it needs to be modified some so its clear by itself without needing to do deep research.

> > If you put new proposal in place, please provide all the changes you made. You force me every time to make the diff, analyze what can be the reasons behind that and assume what is the idea there. It takes a lot of time and the time comes from "moving forward pool".
> 
> This is my whole point. You should not have to do that. If the requirement is so confusing that you need to go back and do deep diff research, then developers reading the requirement will have to do the same - and therefor its not clear enough. _Good requirements should stand strong as they are._ And this one does not. It smells of process. Like really obviously it smells of process, it's in the requirement text itself.

You do realize I was talking about your proposal?

So goals for wording update:
* what must be avoided - that application does not offer functionality (in production) to update it's own code - e.g. installing new modules, themes, plugins, etc or allowing direct modifications. It means, application functionality need to get updates via standard update process.

... but it is pretty close to current wording ...

> > > If you put new proposal in place, please provide all the changes you made. You force me every time to make the diff, analyze what can be the reasons behind that and assume what is the idea there. It takes a lot of time and the time comes from "moving forward pool".
> > 
> > 
> > This is my whole point. You should not have to do that. If the requirement is so confusing that you need to go back and do deep diff research, then developers reading the requirement will have to do the same - and therefor its not clear enough. _Good requirements should stand strong as they are._ And this one does not. It smells of process. Like really obviously it smells of process, it's in the requirement text itself.
> 
> You do realize I was talking about your proposal?

I do, but I am struggling with this one too @elarlang - it's not easy to get this one in as positive, make it verifiable, and not be about process. I am struggling to make this work, that's why my initial suggestion was to just drop it.

> what must be avoided - that application does not offer functionality (in production) to update it's own code - e.g. installing new modules, themes, plugins, etc or allowing direct modifications. It means, application functionality need to get updates via standard update process.

Let me add to this:

* what must be avoided - that application does not offer functionality (in production) to update it's own code, **unless thats a specific feature of a SaaS platform which is done in a sandboxed way on purpose**
* installing new modules, themes, plugins, etc or allowing direct modifications -> **Sometimes this is bad, sometimes is a needed feature of the platform**
* It means, application functionality need to get updates via standard update process. -> **I like standard update process better than "build process"**

So how about something along these lines?

_13.4.3 Verify that application code or functionality can only be changed via the standard update mechanism and not directly in production through application functionality or some other direct modification mechanism, unless it is done in sandboxed way as part of a core SaaS feature like we see in Salseforce and other SaaS platforms._

The salesforce and similar needs to go away, but I am just pointing out a potential direction.

I've had a chance to think this over and show it off to a few architects. Absolutely, I think this must be removed. 

Suppose I can SSH into a server and fix a major problem live. That's zero risk if I do it right. Yet we call this a L2 issue when it's not even testable all the time.

So in summary:

- Very hard to verify
- Not always applicable in serverless, containerized or scripted ops environments
- Enforcement requires policy, not just tooling

Does anyone else care to chime in? @tghosth @danielcuthbert @randomstuff or anyone else?

issue title says: "discussion: development functionality must not be available in production"

Last explanation what I gave: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issuecomment-2815877052

_what must be avoided - **that application does not offer functionality (in production) to update it's own code** - e.g. installing new modules, themes, plugins, etc or allowing direct modifications. It means, application functionality need to get updates via standard update process._

> I've had a chance to think this over and show it off to a few architects. Absolutely, I think this must be removed.

Taking account the history of question asked publicly and the answer below, please let them ask this question from me.

> Suppose I can SSH into a server and fix a major problem live

SSH is not really functionality provided by the application to change it's own code.

Problem to solve here is: if there is session or account takeover it does not escalate to full control over the application.

Hi @jmanico, regarding this:

> unless it is done in sandboxed way as part of a core SaaS feature like we see in Salseforce and other SaaS platforms.

Our general assumption for ASVS requirements is that an application should either comply or explain. Can we not assume in this case that if the application has this functionality built in then the onus is on the application developer to explain that they are not complying but that they have security mechanisms or mitigating controls to avoid the risk?

Trying to keep up with this thread. So we are talking about kind of requirements/propositions:

> 13.4.3 Verify that the running application — including its runtime environment, administration interfaces, and APIs — cannot modify its own executable code or compiled artifacts unless the change is delivered through an authenticated, integrity‑protected update mechanism (e.g, signed packages, secured CI/CD deployment, or the platform’s native version‑controlled update channel).
> 
> 13.4.6 Verify that mechanisms are in place to detect and respond to configuration drift in deployed environments. This may include using immutable infrastructure, automated redeployment from a secure baseline, or drift detection tools that compare current state against approved configurations.

I do agree that it's something you should try to do as much as possible. This kind of secure environment is *very* useful! 

However, I'm not sure we can require if. There are legitimate use cases where manual plugin installation by the application is required (13.4.3). As much as I agree, that we should avoid this as much as possible I don't think we can completely forbid it. It might make more sense in L3 (I would definitely want to have it in an L3 application) but even then I'm not sure we can completely require it.

The same is probably true for the "configuration drift" proposition as they are quite closely related.

Would it make sense to have something such as,

> Verify that the running application cannot modify it's own executable code or configuration unless that is explicitly required for its proper operation.

> However, I'm not sure we can require if. There are legitimate use cases where manual plugin installation by the application is required (13.4.3). 

In production?

I think this discussion here should be reset to the statement in the initial issue: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/1438#issue-1470146918

As I wrote before
> Problem to solve here is: if there is session or account takeover it does not escalate to full control over the application.

If the development functionality is not required and needed for the application work in production, it most likely provide attack vectors, modifying or executing code, seeing more information then needed etc.

> However, I'm not sure we can require if. There are legitimate use cases where manual plugin installation by the application is required (13.4.3). As much as I agree, that we should avoid this as much as possible I don't think we can completely forbid it. It might make more sense in L3 (I would definitely want to have it in an L3 application) but even then I'm not sure we can completely require it.

This is a more eloquent way of explaining the whole point I am making. This is actually quite common in PaaS type services.

> Problem to solve here is: if there is session or account takeover it does not escalate to full control over the application.

This can solved by strong re-authentication/MFA before any app-level production modules can be uploaded live.

(It's quite hard to keep up the state of this conversation, maybe I'm missing some things 😄).

> > Suppose I can SSH into a server and fix a major problem live. That's zero risk if I do it right. Yet we call this a L2 issue when it's not even testable all the time.
>
> SSH is not really functionality provided by the application to change it's own code.

I agree to that. This case is not a development functionality of the application which can be used to takeover control of the application.

The application can execute with an immutable view of the filesystem (eg. `ProtectSystem` and friends), in order to make sure that it cannot possibly update its own code or configuration and you would still be able to SSH into the server and update the application (and even live-hotfix it if you really wanted to).

***

> * Very hard to verify

It's not especially hard to verify. This is not especially hard to verify in white box testing. We might miss some things (as in many other requirements).

It might be more difficult to verify in black box testing though.

> * Not always applicable in serverless, containerized or scripted ops environments

I don't understand this point. This is usually very applicable to serverless, containerized or scripted ops environments. In all these cases, this requirement the applications is typically not going to try to install plugins or update itself so it is usually going to be quite easy to comply with this requirement.

The problem is going to be mostly for more artisanal deployments where software is installed manually and plugins are manually installed (when using Wordpress and stuff)..

> * Enforcement requires policy, not just tooling

When using a CMS such as Wordress it may (depending on how the requirement is formulated) impose a strict development cycle and I think a lot of CMS deployments in the wild don't use a strict development cycle.

***

> If the development functionality is not required and needed for the application work in production, it most likely provide attack vectors, modifying or executing code, seeing more information then needed etc.

Yes definitely. All unneeded/development functionality should be disabled in production environments.

The question is whether plugin installation by the application and application/plugin update by the application itself should always be considered development functionality.

I think these are all fair comments @randomstuff  

My basic summary this, sometimes this kind of functionality is live on purpose with special controls to protect this functionality. Because this is intentional in some services, it makes the requirement awkward to me.

> My basic summary this, sometimes this kind of functionality is live on purpose with special controls to protect this functionality. Because this is intentional in some services, it makes the requirement awkward to me.

Because it is sometimes or somewhere needed (mostly exceptional cases), it is not a good reason to allow it everywhere and for anyone. The same way it is true for the opposite way - although it must be mostly disallowed, there are some reasons to allow it. So it is up to the requirement wording to cover both needs.
